dtz.lead: Most adults who apply for Portuguese nationality or permanent residence have to show Portuguese at level A2. The CIPLE certificate is the usual way to do it. Here you can read about CIPLE A2 and practise with our own mock.
dtz.who.title: Who is this for?
dtz.who.text: CIPLE (Certificado Inicial de Português Língua Estrangeira) is the A2 certificate of CAPLE, the language-assessment centre of the University of Lisbon. It is the usual proof of Portuguese for permanent residence and for naturalisation. Some people are exempt or can use another proof, for example people who went to school in Portugal or who come from a country where Portuguese is the official language. The rules change, so check the official sources before you book. This is general orientation, not legal advice.
dtz.format.note: This is the structure of our own mock, not of the real exam. For the real parts and timings, as far as we could check them, see our CIPLE A2 practice set and CAPLE. The mock has no speaking part: practise that with our speaking tasks. The extra reading & writing tasks are good for more practice.
dtz.scoring.title: How CIPLE A2 is marked
dtz.scoring.text: CAPLE publishes the marking rules, and the result is a pass or a fail. We could not confirm the current pass mark, so check it with CAPLE (to verify). In our mock the point bands are our own guide, not a CAPLE result.

At the end you see your result by part, with our own point bands as a guide. Progress stays saved in the browser.

goethe.lead: The Portuguese as a foreign language certificates of CAPLE, at the University of Lisbon: one exam per level, used for residence, nationality, work and study.
goethe.who.title: Who are the CAPLE exams for?
goethe.who.text: CAPLE has a separate exam for each level: ACESSO (A1), CIPLE (A2), DEPLE (B1), DIPLE (B2), DAPLE (C1) and DUPLE (C2). People take them for work and study, and the CIPLE A2 is the certificate most often used as language proof for residence and Portuguese nationality. Which level is needed, and how old a result may be, is decided by the institution that asks for it, and the rules can change: check with them.

grammatik.artikel.intro: Portuguese has four words for “the”: o, a, os, as. It has four for “a” or “some”: um, uma, uns, umas. After a, de, em and por the article joins the word before it: ao, do, no, pelo.
grammatik.ja-nein-fragen.intro: A yes/no question uses the same words as a statement. Only the question mark and your voice going up show that it is a question. Put não before the verb to say “not”. To answer, repeat the verb: Falas inglês? — Falo.
grammatik.w-fragen.intro: o que, quem, onde, de onde, para onde, quando, como, quanto, qual, porquê. In speech, people in Portugal often add é que after the question word: Onde é que moras?
grammatik.praesens.intro: Portuguese verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir. Take off the ending and add the one for the person: falar → falo, falas, fala. Use the present for now, for habits and for facts.
grammatik.verb-position-2.intro: Portuguese has two verbs for “to be”. Use ser for who or what something is. Use estar for where a person or thing is now and how it is right now: Sou a Ana. Estou em casa. Estou cansada.
grammatik.konjugation.intro: The most useful Portuguese verbs do not follow the rules: ser, estar, ir, ter, fazer, vir. Others are irregular mainly in the eu form: digo, posso, sei, vejo, dou.
grammatik.plural.intro: One house, two houses: after a vowel add -s (casa → casas). After -r, -z and a stressed -s add -es (mulher → mulheres). Words in -m, -l and -ão have their own rules. The article and the adjective become plural too: as casas brancas.
grammatik.possessivartikel.intro: Whose is it? In Portugal the possessive comes with the article: o meu carro, a minha casa, os teus filhos. It matches the thing you have, not the person who has it. For “his” and “her”, people say dele and dela: o carro dele.
grammatik.imperativ.intro: Portuguese has four main forms: tu (fala), você or o senhor (fale), vocês (falem), nós (falemos). Negative forms use the subjunctive: não fales, não fale, não falem. Pronouns go after an affirmative form and before a negative one: diz-me, não me digas.
grammatik.aduso.intro: Use e (and), ou (or), mas (but), porque (because) and por isso (so, that's why) to join words and sentences. Use também for “too” and também não for “not either”. Careful: e = and, é = is.
grammatik.nomen.intro: Every Portuguese noun is masculine or feminine, even a table or a street. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (o livro) and most ending in -a are feminine (a casa). Learn each noun with its article.
grammatik.komposita.intro: To say what is happening right now, use estar + a + infinitive: Estou a trabalhar. Estão a comer. The infinitive never changes, only estar does. English says -ing; Portuguese says a + the infinitive.
grammatik.wortarten.intro: Each word does a job in the sentence. Knowing the job helps you use the word: a noun has a gender, a verb changes for the person, an adjective matches its noun. Two Portuguese specials: prepositions join the article (de + o = do), and small pronouns join the verb with a hyphen (chamo-me).
grammatik.akkusativ.intro: The direct object is the person or thing the verb acts on. Pronouns: me, te, o, a, nos, os, as. In Portugal they usually go after the verb with a hyphen: Vejo a Ana → Vejo-a. After não, já, nunca and question words they go before the verb: Não a vejo.
grammatik.dativ.intro: Indirect object pronouns say who gets something: me, te, lhe, nos, lhes. Dou-lhe o livro. In Portugal the pronoun usually follows the verb with a hyphen. When it meets o, a, os or as, the two join: lhe + o = lho.
grammatik.modalverben.intro: To say what you must, can or want to do, use a conjugated verb + an infinitive: Tenho de trabalhar. Posso ajudar. Quero descansar. É preciso marcar atendimento. The second verb never changes.
grammatik.negation.intro: Put não before the verb: Não trabalho. Portuguese uses double negatives: Não vejo ninguém. Não como nunca carne. If the negative word comes before the verb, drop não: Ninguém vem. Nunca como carne.
grammatik.perfekt.intro: Use the pretérito perfeito simples for finished actions: Ontem falei com o senhorio. Em 2022 chegámos a Portugal. Regular endings: -ei, -aste, -ou for -ar verbs; -i, -este, -eu for -er verbs; -i, -iste, -iu for -ir verbs.
grammatik.satzstellung.intro: muito goes before an adjective or adverb and after a verb, and then it never changes: muito cansado, Trabalho muito. Before a noun it agrees: muita gente, muitos problemas. pouco, bastante, demasiado, tão and tanto follow the same pattern.
grammatik.wechselpraepositionen.intro: Use a or para for movement towards a place: Vou a Lisboa, vou para casa. Use em for being in a place: Estou em Lisboa. With de… a and desde… até you say where a journey or a time starts and ends.
grammatik.positionsverben.intro: These verbs work the other way round from gostar de: the thing or activity is the subject, and the person is a small pronoun (me, te, lhe, nos, lhes). Apetece-me um café. Doem-me os pés. The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person. In Portugal the pronoun usually comes after the verb.
grammatik.praepositionen.intro: Many Portuguese verbs take one fixed preposition: pensar em, sonhar com, depender de, lembrar-se de, precisar de. It often isn't the one English uses, so learn the verb and the preposition together. Before o, a, os, as the preposition contracts: do, da, no, na, ao.
grammatik.trennbare-verben.intro: To talk about plans and the near future, use ir + infinitive: Vou ligar ao médico. Amanhã vamos procurar casa. Only ir changes. The second verb stays in the infinitive. There is no a in between (unlike Spanish voy a or English going to).
grammatik.zusammengesetzte-verben.intro: Many of the most useful verbs are irregular in the pretérito perfeito: ir/ser → fui, ter → tive, estar → estive, fazer → fiz, dizer → disse, vir → vim. They have a new stem and no -ei/-ou endings: Ontem fui ao médico. Tive uma consulta. Fiz o jantar. The regular verbs are in the topic before this one.
grammatik.als-oder-wenn.intro: Both can mean for, but they look in different directions. Para looks ahead: a goal, a person who receives something, a destination, a deadline. Por looks at the cause or the way: why it happens, where it passes, how, at what price. Remember: por + o = pelo, por + a = pela.
grammatik.n-deklination.intro: Use the imperfeito to talk about how things used to be: habits and descriptions in the past. Antes vivia em Rabat. A casa era pequena. -ar verbs take -ava, -er and -ir verbs take -ia. Only four verbs are irregular: ser, ter, vir and pôr.
grammatik.genitiv.intro: To avoid repeating a noun, use the possessive with its article: A minha casa é pequena. E a tua? It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. For his, her and their, say dele, dela, deles, delas: O carro dela é vermelho. After ser, you can drop the article: Este casaco é meu.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination.intro: Most adjectives go after the noun: um carro vermelho. A few can go before it, to give an opinion: uma boa ideia, um mau dia. Bom, mau, primeiro and grande keep one form per gender, but santo becomes são before a masculine name starting with a consonant: São João. Some adjectives change meaning with position: um grande homem, um homem grande.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination-a2.intro: Add -mente to the feminine form of an adjective to make an adverb: rápida → rapidamente, fácil → facilmente. Adverbs describe a verb: Falas bem. Adjectives describe a noun: É um bom médico.
grammatik.ordinalzahlen.intro: Ordinals up to ten are worth knowing: primeiro, segundo, terceiro… They agree with the noun: a segunda rua. Dates use normal numbers: 3 de maio. Floors and addresses use ordinals: rés-do-chão, 1.º andar, 2.º esquerdo.
grammatik.zahlen.intro: From 0 to a million. From 21, join the parts with e: vinte e um, cento e vinte. Um and dois change for feminine nouns: uma hora, duas horas. 100 is cem, 101 is cento e um.
grammatik.adjektive-nach-sein.intro: An adjective matches its noun in gender and number, and it usually comes after the noun: uma casa branca, os carros novos.
grammatik.gern.intro: In Portuguese the person who likes is the subject, as in English: eu gosto de café. gostar is a normal -ar verb and always takes de: gosto de ler, gosto do Porto, gosto da praia.
grammatik.praeteritum-sein-haben.intro: Some common verbs change only in the eu form: pedir → peço, dormir → durmo, vestir → visto, sair → saio, perder → perco. The other persons are almost regular, so learn the eu form with the verb.
grammatik.berufe-mit-in.intro: Use há to say that something exists: Há uma farmácia aqui perto. Use está or estão to say where a known thing is: A farmácia está na praça.
grammatik.konjunktiv2-hoeflich.intro: In Portuguese you are polite with a question and the right verb form: Pode ajudar-me? Podia ajudar-me? To ask for something at an office or shop, use queria or gostava de: Queria marcar uma consulta.
grammatik.infinitiv-mit-zu.intro: The present subjunctive (conjuntivo presente) swaps the vowel: -ar verbs take -e endings (fale), -er and -ir verbs take -a endings (coma, parta). Most irregular forms come from the eu form of the present: tenho → tenha, faço → faça. You will usually see it after que: Quero que venhas.
grammatik.praeteritum-plusquamperfekt.in: In a story, the perfeito simples tells what happened: Cheguei a Lisboa. Tocou o telefone. The imperfeito describes the background and habits: Fazia frio. Vivia num apartamento pequeno. A background action can be interrupted by an event: Dormia quando tocou o despertador.
grammatik.indirekte-fragen.intro: To report in the present, use diz que for statements and pergunta-me se for yes/no questions. Question words stay, with no accent: Não sei onde está. Sabes quando abrem? The word order is simple, and there is no question mark after the indirect part.
grammatik.passiv.intro: In everyday Portuguese, -se after the verb is the normal way to leave out who does something: Aluga-se T2. Vendem-se casas. Vive-se bem aqui. The passive with ser + participle (O edifício foi construído em 1920) belongs mostly to news and formal writing.
grammatik.passiv-b1.intro: Use the mais-que-perfeito for something that had already happened before another moment in the past: Quando cheguei, o comboio já tinha saído. It is tinha + a participle: tinha comido, tinhas chegado, tinham saído.
grammatik.wortbildung-nomen.intro: The ending of a Portuguese noun often tells you what it means and its gender. -ção and -dade make feminine nouns: a informação, a cidade. -mento makes masculine ones: o nascimento. -eiro/-eira is a person with a job, -aria is the shop, -ista works for men and women. -inho and -zinho make things small.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen-b1.in: If something started in the past and is still going on, Portuguese uses the present tense: Moro cá desde 2022 (a starting point). Moro cá há três anos (a period). You can also say Há três anos que moro cá or Faz três anos que moro cá. With a past verb, há means ago.
grammatik.infinitiv-ohne-zu.intro: Ask who does the second action. The same person: use the infinitive (Quero ir). A different person: use que + subjunctive (Quero que vás). Don't say Quero que eu vá.
grammatik.funktionen-von-werden.intro: Use the condicional for polite wishes and requests, advice, and what you would do: Gostaria de marcar uma consulta. Poderia ajudar-me? Eu, no teu lugar, falaria com o senhorio. Add -ia, -ias, -ia, -íamos, -iam to the whole infinitive. In speech, the imperfeito often does the same job.
grammatik.konjunktiv2.intro: Use the imperfeito do conjuntivo when a past verb or the condicional asks for the subjunctive: Queria que viesses. Gostaria que me ligasses. Use it with oxalá for a wish that is unlikely now: Oxalá tivesse mais tempo. To make it, take the eles form of the perfeito, drop -ram and add -sse, -sses, -sse, -ssemos, -ssem.
grammatik.relativpronomen.intro: A relative clause adds information about a noun. Use que for people and things: a rapariga que trabalha comigo, o apartamento que quero. Use onde for places: o bairro onde vivo. After a preposition: a casa em que vivo, a colega com quem falei. Use o que when there is no noun: Não percebo o que ele diz.
grammatik.irgend.intro: Use a verb + me, te, lhe, nos, lhes when something happens to you by accident: Esqueceu-me a carteira. Caiu-me o telemóvel. Avariou-se-me o computador. Acabou-nos o café. The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person.
grammatik.fokuspartikeln.intro: Portuguese has no single verb for “become”. Use pôr-se for a quick change of mood or colour, ficar for the state after an event, tornar-se for a lasting change of character or a profession, passar a ser for a new role or status, and transformar-se em + noun for a big change.
grammatik.negationswoerter.intro: The personal infinitive is the infinitive with person endings: falar, falares, falar, falarmos, falardes, falarem. Use it when the infinitive has its own subject: Para falarmos com calma, vamos à sala. Sem eles saberem, organizámos tudo. É importante estudares.
grammatik.nomen-verb-verbindungen.intro: Some verbs and nouns go together, and another verb sounds wrong: tomar uma decisão, dar um passeio, fazer fila, marcar consulta, ter saudades. English often suggests the wrong verb, so learn the pair as one phrase.
grammatik.partizip-als-adjektiv.intro: Use estar + a participle for the state something is in after an action: A loja está fechada. A carta está escrita. The participle agrees like an adjective: fechado, fechada, fechados, fechadas. A few verbs have two participles: aceitado/aceite, entregado/entregue, ganhado/ganho.
grammatik.adjektive-als-nomen.intro: O + adjective talks about an idea, not a thing or a person: o bom (the good thing), o importante (what matters). The adjective doesn't change. O que means what, the thing that: O que preciso é de tempo. Aquilo que is a stronger form, and o facto de turns a whole situation into a noun.
grammatik.zweiteilige-konnektoren.intro: An opinion you state takes the indicative: Acho que vem. A denied opinion, a doubt or a possibility takes the subjunctive: Não acho que venha. Duvido que venha. É possível que venha. A fact you confirm takes the indicative: É verdade que vem.
grammatik.konditionalsaetze.intro: For a real, possible condition in the future, use se + futuro do conjuntivo: Se chover, fico em casa. Se tiveres tempo, passa por cá. For what is true now or happens every time, use se + present: Se tens febre, vai ao médico. Never use the future after se.
grammatik.konsekutivsaetze.intro: embora, ainda que and mesmo que always take the conjuntivo, whether you state a fact or talk about something unknown: Embora tivesse febre, fui trabalhar. Mesmo que chova, vamos. A consequence: tão cansado que…, tanto trabalho que…, de modo que…
grammatik.zumal-wohingegen.intro: When you report with a past verb (disse que…), the verb usually moves one step back: vivo → vivia, liguei → tinha ligado, virei → viria. Orders and wishes take the imperfect subjunctive: Vai! → Pediu-me que fosse.
grammatik.modalsaetze.intro: For something unreal or unlikely now, use se + imperfeito do conjuntivo, then the condicional: Se tivesse dinheiro, compraria um apartamento. For a past that didn't happen, use se + tivesse + participle, then teria + participle: Se tivesse sabido, teria vindo. In speech the result is often the imperfeito: Se tivesse tempo, ia.
grammatik.reflexive-verben.intro: Many daily-routine verbs need a small pronoun that matches the person: levanto-me, lavas-te, veste-se. In the dictionary the verb ends in -se: levantar-se. In Portugal the pronoun usually comes after the verb, with a hyphen.
grammatik.nebensaetze-weil-dass.intro: Give a reason with porque (after the main idea) or como (at the start). Give a result with por isso, então or portanto. To say what you think or what someone says, use que: Acho que está fechado. Diz que vem amanhã.
grammatik.komparativ-superlativ.intro: To compare, use mais… (do) que, menos… (do) que or tão… como: Este apartamento é mais caro do que o outro. To say “the most”, use o, a, os or as + mais: É o mais barato. Four words have their own forms: melhor, pior, maior, menor.
grammatik.lokale-praepositionen.intro: To say where something is, use estar + a place word: As chaves estão em cima da mesa. Most place words end in de: ao lado de, à frente de, debaixo de. Aqui, aí and ali say how far away it is from you.
grammatik.positionsadverbien.intro: Say how often with sempre, muitas vezes, às vezes, quase nunca and nunca. Use costumar + infinitive for what you usually do: Costumo almoçar às duas. Costumamos ir a pé.
grammatik.personalpronomen.intro: Eu, tu, ele, ela, nós, vocês, eles, elas, plus o senhor / a senhora for a polite “you”. The verb ending already shows the person, so Portuguese often drops the pronoun: Moro em Lisboa.
grammatik.indefinitpronomen.intro: algo is something, nada is nothing. alguém is someone, ninguém is no one. algum and nenhum go with a noun: Há algum problema? Não há nenhum problema. outro means another: outro café.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen.intro: Que horas são? É uma hora. São duas e meia. At what time? Às oito. Use na segunda-feira for “this Monday”, à segunda-feira or às segundas for “on Mondays”, and de manhã for “in the morning”.
grammatik.futur.intro: Portuguese has three ways to talk about the future. The present for fixed plans: Amanhã tenho consulta. Ir + infinitive, the usual spoken future: Vou procurar outra casa. The futuro simples (falarei) for forecasts, formal announcements, promises and guesses: Amanhã choverá. Serão duas horas.
grammatik.temporale-nebensaetze.intro: For things that haven't happened yet, quando, assim que and logo que take the futuro do conjuntivo: Quando chegares, liga-me. For habits and the past, use the indicative: Quando chego, janto. Never use the future after quando.
grammatik.da-wo-woerter.intro: After a preposition, Portuguese uses mim and ti, not eu and tu: para mim, sem ti. The other persons stay the same: com ele, para ela, sem nós. With com there are special forms: comigo, contigo, connosco, consigo. And de or em plus ele or ela contract: dele, nela.
grammatik.lassen.intro: A helper verb + de or a + an infinitive adds a meaning of time: Acabei de comer (a moment ago). Voltei a ligar (again). Deixei de fumar (stopped). Continuo a trabalhar (still). Estou a trabalhar (right now). Learn each one with its little word.
grammatik.modalpartikeln.intro: Small words like então, olha, bem, pois é, pronto and se calhar keep a conversation going: they open, react, hesitate, soften or close. They belong to speech and informal messages, not to a formal email. Pá is very informal and typical of Portugal.
grammatik.adjektive-mit-praepositionen.i: Many adjectives take a fixed preposition: farto de, capaz de, contente com, interessado em, preocupado com, habituado a. Add a noun, an infinitive for the same person, or que + subjunctive for another person.
grammatik.konnektoren-grund-gegengrund.i: Linkers show how two ideas connect. mas = but: Estou cansado, mas vou trabalhar. no entanto = however, além disso = also, por outro lado = on the other hand, portanto and por isso = so, ainda assim = even so. Use a comma after no entanto, além disso, portanto and ainda assim.
grammatik.finalsaetze.intro: To say why you do something, use para. If one person does both actions, use para + infinitive: Estudo para passar no exame. If the second action is someone else's, use para que + subjunctive: Ligo-te para que saibas.
grammatik.zustandspassiv.intro: Careful: tenho trabalhado is NOT the Spanish he hablado or the English I have worked. It means a repeated or continuing action up to now: Ultimamente tenho dormido mal. A single event, even today, takes the perfeito simples: Hoje comi cedo. Ontem fui ao banco.
grammatik.relativsaetze-was-wo.intro: Use the indicative for something you know exists, and the subjunctive for something unknown or that doesn't exist: Conheço alguém que fala russo. Procuro alguém que saiba russo. A preposition goes first: o apartamento em que vivo, a colega com quem falei.
grammatik.konjunktiv-1.intro: The main verb chooses the subjunctive tense. Present main verb: Quero que venhas. Espero que tenhas chegado. Past main verb: Queria que viesses. Lamentei que não tivesse vindo. Tiver feito looks ahead from a future point: Quando tiveres acabado, liga-me.
grammatik.subjektive-modalverben.intro: Small words change the meaning. Dever + infinitive says what is right or probable: Deves pedir marcação. Dever de guesses: Deve de ter quarenta anos. Ter de is a need, haver de a firm promise or fate, vir a means eventually, chegar a means going as far as: Chegou a ser diretor.
grammatik.passiversatz.intro: Portuguese has many ways to set a condition besides se. Caso + subjunctive: Caso precise, ligue-me. Desde que + subjunctive means as long as. A não ser que means unless. No caso de + infinitive is compact: No caso de haver dúvidas, contacte-nos.
grammatik.partizipialattribute.intro: Formal Portuguese has more relatives. O qual follows a preposition or a comma: o motivo pelo qual. O que refers to a whole idea: Não pagou, o que é grave. Cujo means whose and agrees with what follows: a vizinha cujos filhos… Quem, quanto and onde complete the set.
grammatik.nominalisierung.intro: Formal Portuguese often turns a verb or adjective into a noun: subir → a subida, escasso → a escassez, aprovar → a aprovação. A noun phrase such as a subida dos preços says in few words what a full clause says. Everyday speech keeps the verbs.
grammatik.nominale-praepositionen.intro: Letters, reports and contracts link ideas with formal words. Devido a and em virtude de give a cause, ao abrigo de gives a legal basis, no entanto and todavia mark a contrast, por conseguinte a result. Check what comes next: a noun, a clause or a new sentence.
grammatik.irreale-vergleiche.intro: Como se compares something with a situation that isn't real. Same time: imperfect subjunctive, Fala como se soubesse tudo. Earlier: pluperfect subjunctive, Olhou-me como se nunca me tivesse visto. Nem que means even if: Vou, nem que tenha de ir a pé.
grammatik.futur-2.intro: A clause without a conjugated verb says the same thing in fewer words. Ao + infinitive: Ao chegar, vi a carta. The gerund: Vendo que não vinha, liguei-lhe. The participle: Terminada a reunião, saímos. Typical in writing, reports and formal speech.
grammatik.es-korrelat.intro: A cleft sentence puts the spotlight on one part of the message. Use ser + the part in focus + que (or quem for a person): Foi a Ana que ligou. É aqui que moro. Or start with what you want to explain: O que preciso é de tempo.
grammatik.textkohaerenz.intro: A good text holds together. Reference words point back: este, esse, tal, o mesmo, o referido. Isso and o que stand for a whole idea. Ellipsis leaves out what is clear: A Ana vive em Lisboa e o Pedro, no Porto. Register decides which of them you use.
grammatik.verbpraefixe.intro: A prefix changes a word's meaning. Des- undoes it: desfazer. Re- repeats it: reabrir. In- denies: inútil. Sobre- goes over: sobrecarregar. Contra- opposes: contradizer. The 1990 agreement settled the hyphen: antissocial, autoestrada, mas pós-graduação, ex-marido, anti-inflamatório.
grammatik.nutzen-benutzen.intro: Some adjectives change meaning with ser and estar: A aula é aborrecida (boring), Estou aborrecido (annoyed). O Pedro é vivo (sharp), O avô está vivo (alive). Events take ser for their place and time: A festa é na sexta. People and things take estar: A Maria está em casa.
grammatik.verben-als-nomen.intro: After a wish or a feeling about someone else, use que + subjunctive: Quero que venhas. Fico contente que estejas melhor. Oxalá also takes the subjunctive: Oxalá faça sol. For facts and opinions, use the indicative: Acho que vem.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.intro: With gostar de and an ordinary verb, a general thing takes no article: Gosto de café. Bebo água. Tenho carro. No article for jobs and languages either: É médica. Falo português. But names and possessives take one: o Pedro, a minha mãe.
grammatik.welcher-dieser.intro: This one, that one, that one over there: este is near me, esse is near you, aquele is far from us both. They match the noun: esta casa, esses livros. Isto, isso and aquilo name something without a noun. After de and em they join up: deste, nesta, daquele, nisso.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.brief:
Why “Gosto de café” with no article? Why “É médica”, but “a minha mãe”?

  • —No article: jobs, languages, general things after gostar de, tenho, bebo.
  • um, umaOne of many, or a new thing: há uma farmácia.
  • o, aThe one we both know, names, possessives, days of the week.

home.mock.pronNote.0: Men say obrigado, women say obrigada. The final o sounds like a short u: o-bri-GA-du.
home.mock.pronNote.1: One r between vowels is a single quick tap; rr is a strong sound at the back of the throat in Lisbon. They are different words.
home.mock.pronNote.2: om is a nasal vowel: say o through the nose, without closing the lips for a full m.
home.mock.pronNote.3: In Portugal, s before a consonant or at the end of a word sounds like “sh”: ush pash-TÉISH.
home.mock.pronNote.4: An unstressed e is very short or dropped in Portugal: u t'le-MÓ-vel.

kultur.sourcingNote:
Every topic here is factual knowledge: publicly checkable facts about rules, institutions and procedures in Portugal (laws, who is responsible, what you do), written by icanspeak Portuguese from official sources such as the Diário da República, the ePortugal public services portal and the ministries. Portugal comes first; the topics on the wider Portuguese-speaking world follow.
What is deliberately NOT here: claims about “the Portuguese character”. Nothing is claimed about people; rules, figures and responsibilities are, and where practice differs between the mainland, Madeira and the Azores, between municípios or between people, the topic says so.
Rules and figures change. A figure carries its date; if in doubt, the official source is right, not this page. This is general orientation, not legal advice.

akk.regel.intro: The direct object is the person or thing the verb acts on: Vejo a Ana. Vejo a casa. In Portugal the pronoun usually goes after the verb, joined with a hyphen: Vejo-a. After não, question words, que and some adverbs (já, também, ainda, nunca) it moves before the verb: Não a vejo.
akk.regel.example: Common mistake: A vejo. → Vejo-a. In Portugal a sentence never starts with the pronoun (Spanish speakers, watch out). After -r, -s, -z the verb loses that letter and o, a become lo, la: Quero ver + a → Quero vê-la. After a nasal sound they become no, na: Dão-no.

sets.prog.title: Your progress
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.1: Full sentences, not a list: “Tenho 29 anos.”, not just “29”. Age goes with ter, and a job takes no article: “Sou eletricista.”
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.2: End with your free time: it is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.0: “Na fotografia vejo …” is the easiest way to start. Portuguese needs no little word before people: vejo uma mulher, vejo um comboio.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.1: “Acho que …” and “se calhar …” let you guess without being sure.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.2: The last sentence is about you: that is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.0: First count (“duas pessoas”), then say the place, then the action. This order always works.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.1: For what is happening now, use estar a + infinitive: está a cozinhar, está a comer. (Brazilians say está cozinhando.)
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.0: Fruta is usually singular in Portuguese: compro fruta. But maçãs and bananas are plural.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.1: “na caixa”, “com cartão”, “em dinheiro”: learn the little word with the phrase.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.2: A time phrase at the end (“ao sábado”, “uma vez por semana”) sounds practised straight away.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.0: Two people, two descriptions: first the boy, then the girl.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.1: One sentence about the weather: está bom tempo, está sol, está calor, faz calor.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.2: “porque” joins your reason to your sentence: gosto do parque porque é tranquilo.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-nachbarschaftsfes: Say what is em primeiro plano and ao fundo: that is the step from A1 to A2.
A guess with a reason: “Acho que é …, porque …”
End with a comparison with your own life or country. At A2 a comparison like this is a natural last step.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.0: Say how someone feels and why: “Parece preocupada. Se calhar …” Pictures with people often invite this question.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.1: Say what you can and can't see: “Só vemos o braço dele.”
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.2: A real detail from your own life (“às vezes espero uma semana”) is worth more than a general sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-bewerbungsgesprae: Use place words to organise what you say: à esquerda, à direita, do outro lado de, ao fundo.
Show that a guess is a guess (“Diria que …”, “pode ser que esteja …”) and give a reason.
The part in the past is expected at B1: the pretérito perfeito for the event (“fiz”), the pretérito imperfeito for how you felt (“estava”).
One sentence with “Na minha opinião”: giving your opinion is the real B1 part.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.0: “Suponho que …, porque …” joins a guess and a reason in one sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.1: Explain a word (curso profissional) instead of just saying it.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.2: The “porquê?” question gets a real answer with “porque” or “Uma razão poderia ser que …”.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.0: Show how you know something: “Nota-se que …, porque …”
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.1: Give a real example from your own life instead of a general complaint.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.2: “Agora …” shows how things have changed, which is a useful B1 skill.
You react to the other person instead of working through your own list.
Disagree politely at least once: that is what the task tests.
At the end you clearly agree on every point.
Polite forms with the conditional: proporia, escolheria, poderíamos …
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.0: The description is short. At B2 it is the way in, not the task.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.1: Both sides are there, with the linking words for them: uma vantagem clara, por outro lado, não podemos esquecer.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.2: Saying “não é só …, é também …” shows you have really thought the question through.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.3: The personal ending is honest rather than perfect: that is harder to say and sounds more mature.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.0: Something you notice in the picture supports your argument (“O que me chama a atenção é que …”), not just general knowledge.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.1: The objection to your own view is there (“Alguns dirão que …”) and you answer it.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.2: The difference between “dias de escritório para toda a equipa” and “uma regra para cada pessoa” is a fine distinction. That is exactly what separates B2 from B1.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-baustelle-innenst: A detail from the picture (the flats right next to the site) becomes part of the argument, not just a description.
“A verdadeira questão não é se …, mas como …” moves the discussion on: a strong B2 phrase.
The opinion ends with conditions, not a simple yes or no. That is more balanced and easier to defend.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.0: A system is explained, not just judged.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.1: The counter-argument and your answer to it are both there.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.2: “Reciclar limita os danos; não resolve o problema”: a short, sharp sentence at the end stays with the listener.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.3: The comparison with your own country doesn't judge; it describes a difference.

mhelp.aria: Help: what is this page for?
mhelp.kultur.what: Here you learn how everyday life in Portugal works: meal times, the Junta de Freguesia, the centro de saúde, public holidays and much more.
mhelp.kultur.s1: Pick a topic at your level (A1, A2 …).
mhelp.kultur.s2: Read the short text and look at the examples.
mhelp.kultur.s3: Then answer the quiz questions. That way you remember what matters.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.what: Etymology is the story of a word: where it comes from, how it used to sound and what it used to mean. Portuguese words come from Latin, Arabic, Celtic and Germanic languages, Tupi and more, so some may be related to words in your language.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s1: “The root” shows the oldest form of the word we know.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s2: Read the family tree from the bottom up: from the root to the words of today.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s3: “Tracing it in other languages” shows the word in your language. Tip: tap the speaker to hear the word.
mhelp.grammatik.what: Every grammar topic, sorted by level — each with a rule and exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s1: Choose your level and a topic, or follow the guided path to go step by step in the right order.
mhelp.grammatik.s2: Read the rule first, then do the exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s3: Your results are saved. You can see them under „Mein Fortschritt“.
mhelp.hoeren.what: Practise listening: announcements, phone calls, conversations and radio pieces from A1 to B2.
mhelp.hoeren.s1: Choose a text at your level.
mhelp.hoeren.s2: Listen as often as you like — slower, too.
mhelp.hoeren.s3: Answer the questions. Afterwards the transcript helps you.
mhelp.lesen.what: Practise reading with real kinds of text: signs, adverts, emails and articles.
mhelp.lesen.s1: Choose a task at your level.
mhelp.lesen.s2: Read the text calmly. There is no rush.
mhelp.lesen.s3: Answer the questions and read the explanation for each answer.
mhelp.sprechen.what: Practise speaking as in the exam: describe pictures, introduce yourself, plan together, discuss.
mhelp.sprechen.s2: Start the timer and speak out loud. The useful phrases help you.
mhelp.sprechen.s3: Afterwards, compare with the model answer.
mhelp.uebungen.what: Your overview: all exercises and your progress in one place.
mhelp.uebungen.s1: At the top you see where you are right now.
mhelp.uebungen.s2: Choose an area: grammar, vocabulary, listening, reading or speaking.
mhelp.uebungen.s3: “Keep practising” takes you straight to the next task.
mhelp.aussprache.what: Train your pronunciation: listen to words and sentences, repeat them and record yourself.
mhelp.aussprache.s2: Listen to the word and say it after the speaker.
mhelp.aussprache.s3: Record yourself and compare with the original.

nsw.why.p1: Nobody learns every form by heart – native speakers look things up too. If you know where the answer is, you write with more confidence and don't have to guess.

sprachen.title: Portuguese around the world
sprachen.lead: Where Portuguese is spoken, on four continents, which languages it is related to, and how close your first language is to Portuguese.
sprachen.stat.official: countries with Portuguese as an official language, plus Macau
sprachen.stat.eu: most spoken language of the Southern Hemisphere
sprachen.map.title: Where Portuguese is spoken
sprachen.map.lead: Tap a country or a dot. The colours show how Portuguese is used there.
sprachen.map.empty: Pick a country on the map, or in the list below.
sprachen.legend.region: Official, beside other languages at home
sprachen.benrath.text: Portuguese began in the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula, as one language with Galician, and sailed with the explorers from the 15th century. Most speakers now live in Brazil. In Africa it is official in five countries and in Equatorial Guinea, in Asia in Timor-Leste and Macau. Switch to the Atlantic view for a closer look at Africa and the islands.
sprachen.count.native: people have Portuguese as their first language
sprachen.count.dialect: people can hold a conversation in Portuguese
sprachen.count.note: Rounded estimate; see the sources at the end of the page.
sprachen.c.PRT: Where Portuguese began, and the variety this course teaches: European Portuguese. It is the official language of the whole country; Mirandese is also officially recognised, in the Terra de Miranda. Accents change from the Minho to the Algarve and on the islands: see the accent map.
sprachen.c.BRA: The country with by far the most Portuguese speakers: more than 200 million. Brazilian Portuguese differs from the European variety in sound, in some grammar (você, the gerund, pronouns before the verb) and in many everyday words. Hundreds of thousands of Brazilians live in Portugal, so you will hear it every day.
sprachen.c.STP: Portuguese is official and the first language of most people on the two islands. Creoles such as Forro are still spoken, mostly by older people. Leve-leve, ‘take it easy’, sums up the pace of life.
sprachen.c.AGO: Portuguese is official and, above all in Luanda, the first language of many young people. Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo are widely spoken too. Angolan words like bué and kota have travelled into Lisbon slang.
sprachen.c.MOZ: Portuguese is official and the language of school and the cities, but most people grow up with a Bantu language such as Makhuwa, Sena or Changana. Many people also speak English, the language of most neighbouring countries.
sprachen.c.GNB: Portuguese is official and the language of school, law and writing, but most people use Guinea-Bissau Creole (Kriol) as their common language, beside Balanta, Fula, Mandinka and others.
sprachen.c.CPV: Portuguese is official and used at school, in writing and in the media; at home people speak Cape Verdean Creole (Kriolu). A large share of Cape Verdeans live abroad, many of them in Portugal and the United States.
sprachen.c.TLS: Portuguese and Tetum are the official languages. Portuguese came back after independence in 2002 as a language of law and school; Tetum, full of Portuguese words, is what people speak every day.
sprachen.c.GNQ: Portuguese became an official language in 2010, beside Spanish and French, before the country joined the CPLP, the community of Portuguese-speaking countries, in 2014. Few people speak it. On the island of Annobón people speak Fa d'Ambô, a Portuguese-based creole.
sprachen.c.MAC: A Chinese special administrative region, and under Portuguese administration until 1999. Portuguese is still co-official beside Chinese and is used on street signs and in the law, but only a small part of the population speaks it.
sprachen.c.FRA: Home to one of the largest Portuguese communities abroad, from the emigration of the 1960s and 1970s. Hundreds of thousands of people in France speak Portuguese at home, and some schools teach it.
sprachen.c.CHE: Portuguese is one of the most spoken foreign languages in Switzerland, thanks to the many workers from Portugal, above all in the French-speaking west.
sprachen.c.LUX: A small country with a very large Portuguese community: around one resident in seven is a Portuguese citizen. You hear Portuguese in shops, cafés and on building sites every day.
sprachen.c.GBR: A large and growing community from Portugal, Madeira, Brazil and the African countries, above all in London. Jersey in the Channel Islands has a long-standing Madeiran community.
sprachen.c.USA: Portuguese emigration goes back to the whaling ships of the 19th century. New England, Newark and California have old Azorean and mainland communities, and many Brazilians have settled more recently, above all in Massachusetts and Florida.
sprachen.c.CAN: Many Portuguese Canadians, a large part of them from the Azores, live in Toronto and Montreal. Toronto's Little Portugal is one of the best-known Portuguese neighbourhoods abroad.
sprachen.m.goa: Portuguese territories until 1961. Few people speak Portuguese there today, mostly older people, but family names, churches, food and many Konkani words recall that time.
sprachen.m.malaca: In Malacca, Malaysia, a small community still speaks Papiá Kristang, a Portuguese-based creole that goes back to the 16th century.
sprachen.m.uruguai: Along the border with Brazil, many people in northern Uruguay grow up with a local Portuguese, mixed with Spanish and known as portuñol or the Portuguese dialects of Uruguay.
sprachen.tree.title: The language family
sprachen.tree.lead: Portuguese is a Romance language: it grew out of the Latin spoken in the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula, where it began as one language with Galician. Romance belongs to the large Indo-European family, so many languages from Iceland to India share distant roots with it.
sprachen.tree.otherLead: These languages are not related to Portuguese, though several of them live beside it in Brazil, Africa and Asia and have lent it words: ananás and jacaré come from Tupi. That doesn't make Portuguese harder: it just means you learn words fresh rather than recognising them.
sprachen.tree.names: Language names are given in English. The tree is simplified: Mirandese and Asturian belong to the Astur-Leonese group, and the creoles have Portuguese words but a grammar of their own.
sprachen.cmp.title: How close is your language?
sprachen.cmp.lead: Pick your first language. Eight basic words show how much you already bring with you.
sprachen.cmp.fehler: Typical mistakes with this first language
sprachen.cmp.englisch: English is Germanic, but it took thousands of words from French and Latin, so you can already read a lot of Portuguese: hospital, animal, possível. The word decoder below shows the patterns. Watch out for false friends: puxar means to pull, and constipado means you have a cold.
sprachen.cmp.deutsch: German is Germanic, a distant relative of Portuguese: Mutter – mãe, drei – três. You already know grammatical gender and verb endings, which helps. Portuguese has only two genders and no noun cases, but it has more past tenses, a subjunctive you will use every day, and nasal vowels (pão, mãe) that take practice.
sprachen.cmp.franzoesisch: French is a close relative. Much of the grammar will feel familiar: articles, gender, the subjunctive, and even nasal vowels. The new parts are the vowels that almost vanish in European Portuguese and the final s that sounds like sh. Watch out: pretender means to intend, not to claim.
sprachen.cmp.spanisch: The closest big relative of Portuguese: all eight words share a root, and you can read a lot from day one. The hard part is listening: European Portuguese swallows its unstressed vowels. Watch out for false friends: esquisito means strange (Spanish exquisito is delicious), and in Portugal apelido is your surname. Mixing the two languages (portunhol) is easy and hard to unlearn.
sprachen.cmp.italienisch: Italian is a close relative, with similar verbs and many shared words: notte – noite, nome – nome. Watch out for false friends: Portuguese salsa is parsley, and Italian salire means to climb, while sair means to go out. Portuguese uses ser and estar where Italian mostly has essere, and its nasal vowels are new.
sprachen.cmp.rumaenisch: Romanian is also Romance, although it has been surrounded by Slavic languages for centuries: noapte – noite, apă – água. Portuguese nouns have no cases, and the article goes before the noun: a casa, where Romanian says casa. The weak, short vowels of European Portuguese will remind you of ă.
sprachen.cmp.arabisch: Arabic belongs to the Afro-Asiatic family and is not related to Portuguese. But after centuries of al-Andalus, Portuguese is full of Arabic words: azeite (az-zayt), açúcar (as-sukkar), almofada, oxalá. Many place names in the south come from Arabic too: Algarve is al-gharb, ‘the west’.
sprachen.cmp.russisch: Russian is Slavic, another branch of the same family: мать – mãe, три – três. Portuguese nouns have no cases, but there are articles (o, a), which Russian doesn't have. The weak unstressed vowels of European Portuguese will feel familiar: Russian reduces them too.
sprachen.cmp.ukrainisch: Ukrainian is Slavic and distantly related to Portuguese: ніч – noite, три – três. Portuguese nouns have no cases, so word order and prepositions do that job, and articles (o, a) are new. Portugal has a large Ukrainian community, so many people have made this journey before you.
sprachen.cmp.chinesisch: Chinese is Sino-Tibetan and not related to Portuguese. Good news: Portuguese has no tones, and its spelling mostly tells you how to say a word. The big new step is verbs: every person and tense has its own ending. And chá came into Portuguese from Chinese, through the trade with Macau.
sprachen.cmp.note: Being related helps with vocabulary. For grammar and pronunciation, practice is what counts.
sprachen.dec.title: English → Portuguese: the word decoder
sprachen.dec.lead: English took thousands of words from Latin and French, and Portuguese grew out of Latin. So many long English words are really Portuguese words in disguise. If you know English, these patterns let you guess a lot of Portuguese.
sprachen.dec.step1: At the top is a pattern: English on the left, Portuguese on the right.
sprachen.dec.step2: Below are examples: English word → Portuguese word.
sprachen.dec.step3: Try it with a word you know: swap the pattern and say it. Often you get a real Portuguese word, and people will understand you.
sprachen.dec.note: They're rules of thumb: not every word fits (difference is diferença), and accents have to be learned (nação, público, económico). Watch out for false friends: atualmente means currently, sensível means sensitive, and a pasta is a folder.
sprachen.dec.quiz: Try it yourself: what is it in Portuguese?

sprachen.src.text: Figures are rounded. Speaker totals: the usual estimates of Camões, I.P. and the CPLP, about 260 million speakers in total; figures differ by source and year. dialekte.title: Accents of Portuguese in Portugal
dialekte.lead: From the Minho to the Algarve, and out to the Azores and Madeira: how Portuguese sounds in different parts of Portugal, which other languages you will meet there, and how Brazil and Africa differ. Pick a region for examples and typical words.
dialekte.map.title: The accent map
dialekte.map.lead: The colours show five groups: the north, the centre with Lisbon and Coimbra, the south, the Azores and Madeira. The dots are two well-known city accents and Portugal's other languages. The islands are moved into boxes; the Azores are drawn smaller than they are, because they spread over some 600 km of ocean.
dialekte.map.empty: Click a region or a dot on the map.
dialekte.map.wordNote: Simplified: in many places you hear several forms, and the borders between them are not sharp. Um café and uma imperial are understood everywhere.
dialekte.group.norte.text: v and b often sound the same (binho for vinho), ou stays a real diphthong, and older speakers keep sounds the rest of the country has lost, such as tch in chuva.
dialekte.group.centro.text: Lisbon and Coimbra are the base of standard European Portuguese, the pronunciation this course teaches: unstressed vowels almost disappear, ou is said as ô, and v and b are two different sounds. Lisbon's ei sounds like ‘ay’ (lâite).
dialekte.group.sul.text: Slower, more open speech with a melody of its own. ei becomes a plain ê (pêxe), and many people use the gerund as Brazilians do: tou fazendo for estou a fazer.
dialekte.group.acores.text: Island accents that change from island to island. São Miguel's is famous for being hard to follow, even for people from Lisbon: rounded vowels like French u and a strong melody.
dialekte.group.madeira.text: A melodic accent with gliding vowels, and island words such as semilha for potato.
dialekte.r.minho: The north-west, around Porto and Braga. Many people here say v like b (o binho, a baca for a vaca), keep the ou in pouco, and speak with a quick, strong melody. Porto has words of its own: um fino, um cimbalino, a francesinha. Learn to hear them, and use the standard forms yourself.
dialekte.r.transmontano: Trás-os-Montes, ‘behind the mountains’, is the most conservative region. Older speakers say tch for ch (a tchuva), make the s with the tip of the tongue and say v like b. In the far east, around Miranda do Douro, a different language is spoken too: Mirandese.
dialekte.r.beiras: Coimbra, Aveiro and the inland Beiras. Coimbra's speech is often called the ‘best Portuguese’; that is a myth, but its vowels are clear and its ei keeps an e (lêite). The inland north, Beira Alta, sounds more northern, with b for v in many villages.
dialekte.r.lisboa: The Portuguese of the TV news, of offices and of this course. Unstressed vowels almost disappear (telefone sounds like ‘t'lfon’), ei sounds like ‘ay’ (lâite, pâixe), and a final s sounds like sh (as casas). Young Lisboners use a lot of slang, some of it from Angola and Brazil: bué, fixe, curtir.
dialekte.r.alentejo: Wide plains and a slow, sung way of speaking that the rest of the country loves to joke about. ei becomes ê (pêxe, lête), então is often atão, and the gerund is normal: tou fazendo. Cante alentejano, the region's choral singing, is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.
dialekte.r.algarve: The south coast. Close to the Alentejo, with the gerund and a plain ê, and words of its own: moce for a young man, marafado for annoyed. In summer you hear every language here, and many people switch to English with foreigners: ask them to stay in Portuguese.
dialekte.r.acores: Nine islands in the middle of the Atlantic, and nearly as many accents. On São Miguel the u sounds like French u (tüdo) and the melody is strong; Terceira and the western islands are easier for Lisbon ears. Many Azoreans emigrated to the United States and Canada, so you also hear Azorean Portuguese in Massachusetts and Toronto.
dialekte.r.madeira: A gliding, melodic accent and words of its own: semilha for batata, poncha for the island drink. Funchal is easier to follow than the villages. Many Madeirans emigrated to Venezuela, South Africa and Jersey.
dialekte.m.porto: Porto speech is loud, warm and direct, with b for v and a lot of humour. Friendly swearing like carago is part of it; you do not need to copy that. Even the coffee has its own name here: um cimbalino.
dialekte.m.lisboa-cidade: Lisbon speech is the model for the standard and the source of much slang. A Lisboner is an alfacinha. The capital mixes the whole country with Brazil, Angola, Cape Verde and many other places, so you hear every variety of Portuguese in its streets.
dialekte.m.mirandes: Mirandese (mirandés) is officially recognised by Portuguese law since 1999. It is related to Asturian and Leonese in Spain; it is a language of its own, not a dialect of Portuguese. A few thousand people speak it, many of them older, and local schools offer it as a subject. Portugal also recognises Portuguese Sign Language (LGP) in its Constitution.
dialekte.m.barranquenho: Spoken in Barrancos, a small town on the Spanish border in the Alentejo: Portuguese mixed with the Spanish of Extremadura and Andalusia, grown over centuries of life on the border. A law of 2021 recognises and protects it.
dialekte.m.minderico: The old secret trade language of the wool and blanket makers of Minde: Portuguese grammar with words of its own, so outsiders could not follow a deal. Only a small group still speaks it, and local projects work to keep it alive.
dialekte.lines.title: Two lines across Portugal
dialekte.lines.lead: Two sound differences explain much of what you hear. The lines on the map show roughly where they run. Real borders are wide and blurred, and younger people, above all in the cities, sound more like Lisbon than their grandparents do.
dialekte.lines.benrath.title: The b/v line: vinho | binho
dialekte.lines.benrath.text: North of the line, many people say v and b the same way, so o vinho sounds like o binho and a vaca like a baca. South of it, v and b are two sounds, as in English. Northerners joke about it themselves. The spelling never changes: everyone writes vinho.
dialekte.lines.speyer.title: The ei line: peixe | pêxe
dialekte.lines.speyer.text: South and east of the line, in the Alentejo and the Algarve, ei often becomes a plain ê: pêxe, lête, primêro. North and west of it you hear a diphthong: ‘ay’ in Lisbon (pâixe), ‘ey’ in Coimbra and the north (pêixe). The Lisbon ‘ay’ is the sound this course teaches.
dialekte.lines.note: Simplified: inside every group there are many local accents, and the same person may speak differently at work and at home. The spelling never changes: everyone writes vinho, peixe and chuva.
dialekte.world.title: Portuguese beyond Portugal
dialekte.world.lead: This course teaches European Portuguese, but your neighbours, colleagues and favourite series may speak another variety. They all understand each other and write almost the same way; the 1990 Orthographic Agreement brought the spellings closer, though not every country has adopted it. Brazil differs most: você in place of tu, the gerund (estou falando), pronouns before the verb (me dá), open vowels and many everyday words (ônibus, trem, celular, café da manhã). The African varieties stay close to the European norm in grammar.
dialekte.w.brasil: More than 200 million speakers, so most of the Portuguese you hear online is Brazilian. The vowels are open and clear, which makes it easier to follow at first; a final -te or -de often sounds like ‘tchi’ or ‘dji’. Você is the everyday ‘you’, and the pronoun goes first: Me liga! Many Brazilians live in Portugal, so you will hear both varieties every day.
dialekte.w.angola: Portuguese is the first language of a large part of the population, above all in Luanda. It follows the European norm in grammar but has its own rhythm and many words from Kimbundu and Umbundu, such as kota. Angolan music, from semba to kuduro and kizomba, carries its slang to Lisbon.
dialekte.w.mocambique: Portuguese is official and the language of school, the cities and offices, but most people grow up with an African language such as Makhuwa, Sena or Changana. Mozambican Portuguese is close to the European norm, with words of its own like chapa and machimbombo.
dialekte.w.caboverde: Portuguese is official and used at school, in writing and on the news; at home almost everyone speaks Cape Verdean Creole (Kriolu), which grew out of Portuguese and West African languages. Its music, from morna to funaná, travels the world, and many Cape Verdeans live in Lisbon.
dialekte.w.guine: Portuguese is official but spoken by a minority. Guinea-Bissau Creole (Kriol) is the language most people share, beside Balanta, Fula, Mandinka and others.
dialekte.w.saotome: Portuguese is the first language of most people, more than anywhere else in Africa. Local creoles such as Forro, Angolar and Lung'ie are still spoken, mostly by older people.
dialekte.w.timor: Portuguese and Tetum are both official. Portuguese came back as a language of school and law after independence in 2002; Tetum, full of Portuguese words, is the everyday language. Indonesian and English are common too.
dialekte.learn.title: Do I have to learn an accent?
dialekte.learn.text: No. Use the European Portuguese you learn here: it is understood everywhere and works in every exam, office and workplace in Portugal. Regional sounds are not mistakes, so there is no need to correct people or to change how you speak. If you live in Porto or Faro, train your ear first: learn to hear vinho in binho and peixe in pêxe. And when someone switches to English with you, it is fine to ask: Podemos falar em português?
dialekte.src.title: Sources
dialekte.src.text: A simplified overview following the usual descriptions of European Portuguese dialects (Lindley Cintra's classification, the Atlas Linguístico-Etnográfico de Portugal e da Galiza, Instituto Camões). Mirandese: Lei n.º 7/99. Barranquenho: recognised by law in 2021. Portuguese Sign Language: Constitution, article 74. Real accent borders are fluid; the areas and lines are drawn roughly and the islands by hand. Coast outlines: Natural Earth (public domain). As of November 2026.

satzmelodie.lead: Same words, a different melody: at the end of the sentence your voice goes down ↘ or up ↗. Listen, compare and repeat.

satzmelodie.task1.title: Listen and compare the melody.
satzmelodie.task1.text: Repeat after me: after each sentence you have time to say it out loud. With the microphone 🎤 next to a sentence you can check your own melody – the recording stays on your device.
satzmelodie.caveat: Careful, echo question ↗↗: in Portuguese, “A Ana vem amanhã?” and “A Ana vem amanhã.” have the same words, so the melody is what makes it a question. A normal yes/no question rises a little at the end. An echo question rises much higher, and it means something different: you're surprised or checking that you heard right (“Como? Vem amanhã?”).
satzmelodie.mic.title: Repeat and check
satzmelodie.task2.title: Listen. Statement, question or exclamation?
satzmelodie.task2.text: The words are always the same. Only the melody is different. Add the punctuation marks.
satzmelodie.task3.title: Which word is stressed? Click it.
satzmelodie.task3.text: The answer is always the same sentence. The question decides which word gets the stress.
satzmelodie.task4.title: Melody maze: which exit?
satzmelodie.task4.text: Quaki hops through the sentence with the voice. At the end the path splits: does the voice go up, down, or steeply down? Then you see the real melody – and Quaki rides along it.
satzmelodie.lab.aria: Maze: at the end of the sentence the path splits into three exits – top: question, bottom: statement, very bottom: exclamation.
satzmelodie.rule.title: The melody at the end of the sentence
satzmelodie.rule.aussage: The voice falls at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.w: The voice usually falls at the end, as in a statement. Questions with o que, onde, quando, quem, como, porquê, quanto and qual. In everyday speech you often hear quando é que, onde é que. With a gentle rise instead, they sound extra friendly.
satzmelodie.rule.jn: Usually the same words as a statement: only the melody, and the ? in writing, makes it a question. The voice rises at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.echo: The voice rises high at the end. You're surprised or checking what you heard. You can start it with Então or Ai é? and repeat the part you did not believe.
satzmelodie.rule.ausruf: The stressed word goes very high, then the voice falls a long way. Feeling: joy, anger, surprise.
satzmelodie.rule.liste: The voice stays level → until the list is finished. Then it falls ↘.
satzmelodie.teacherTip: For teachers: a pair activity with three cards (. ? !). A says “A Ana vem amanhã” with one melody, B holds up the matching card.
satzmelodie.res.noRecorder: Your browser can't record here. Try Chrome, Edge or Safari.
satzmelodie.res.noMic: It doesn't work without a microphone: allow access in the address bar and tap the microphone again.
satzmelodie.res.speak: Speak now: “{text}” – tap the microphone when you're done.
satzmelodie.res.tooQuiet: I hardly heard anything. Speak a bit louder and closer to the microphone.
satzmelodie.res.echoTip: In an echo question the voice goes up sharply at the end, even more clearly than in a yes/no question.
satzmelodie.res.endQuiet: The end of the sentence was too quiet to judge.
satzmelodie.res.noModel: There's no recording for this sentence yet – so only the end of the sentence is checked.
satzmelodie.res.failed: The recording couldn't be analysed. Try again.
satzmelodie.why.aussage: Statement: the voice goes down at the end ↘.
satzmelodie.why.echo: Echo question: the voice goes clearly up at the end ↗. You're surprised or checking that you heard right. A normal yes/no question rises much less.
satzmelodie.why.ausruf: Exclamation: the voice starts high and falls sharply ↘. You're excited or surprised.
satzmelodie.stress.ok: Correct! This word is the new information.
satzmelodie.stress.again: Try again: which word answers the question directly?

wissen.lernen.lead: Mistakes are allowed. Even more: without mistakes you learn more slowly. Here Bruno, Regi, Hamsti and Quaki explain how your brain really holds on to Portuguese.
wissen.lernen.jungle.title: Your brain is a jungle
wissen.lernen.jungle.lead: Imagine this: a new word lies on the other side of a dense jungle. There's no path to it yet. You have to cut it yourself.
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.title: The machete
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.text: Learning is your machete. On your first try you hack your way through the jungle with effort. That's tiring – and completely normal.
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.title: The wrong way
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.text: Sometimes you walk in the wrong direction: a mistake. Your brain notices the difference between what it expected and the right answer. That very signal shows it where the path really goes.
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.title: The beaten path
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.text: Every time you walk the path again, it gets wider. Nerve cells that often work together connect more strongly.
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.title: The road
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.text: After many repetitions the path has become a road. You don't have to think anymore – the word is just there. Practice even changes the wiring in your brain along the way.
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot1: And a path you don't walk for a long time? It slowly grows over again. That's why you repeat (Rule 3).
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot2: Your brain constantly rebuilding itself like this is called neuroplasticity. Adults who learn to juggle for three months have measurably more grey matter afterwards
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot4: And London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot5: Your brain learns at any age.
wissen.lernen.wheel.label: The seven rules
wissen.lernen.wheel.title: The learning circle
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.title: Making mistakes is part of it
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.text: You're not supposed to get everything right straight away. If you try an answer, get it wrong and then see the right one, you remember it better than if you only read it.
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.why: A mistake surprises your brain. That surprise makes the correction stick. Even mistakes you were completely sure about get corrected especially well afterwards. The only important thing: always look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.say: Hmm … what was it called again?
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.title: Recall first, then check
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.text: Reading a word list five times feels good – but doesn't do much. Better: cover the word and quiz yourself. Only then do you check.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.why: Every time you pull a word out of your head, the path to it gets wider. Reading only goes through your eyes. Remembering is work, and that very work is what stays.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.title: A little, but often – and sleep well
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.text: Ten minutes every day are better than two hours on Sunday. And when you've almost forgotten a word, that's the best moment to review it.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.why: With breaks between reviews, knowledge stays much longer. While you sleep, your brain sorts what you learned during the day. So learning in the evening and a quick review in the morning go well together.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.title: Mix instead of blocks
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.text: Twenty sentences with only the present tense are easy – you already know what's coming. In real life you don't. So mix it up: present, past and future, all jumbled.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.why: When you mix, you learn not only the rule but also when you need it. That's harder, but it's exactly what you need in conversation and in the exam.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.title: Speak out loud, don't just read
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.text: Read new sentences out loud. Speak along when you listen to audio. Even alone in the kitchen – that's not weird, that's training.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.why: What you say out loud, you also hear, and you move your mouth while doing it. So your head remembers the sentence in several ways. And your mouth learns the words before you need them in a conversation.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.title: It can be hard – but not too hard
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.text: If everything is easy, you learn little. If everything is too hard, you give up. You learn the most in between: you have to think, but you usually manage.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.why: The effort isn't a sign that you're bad at it. It's the sign that you're learning right now. Choose your level so that you get about eight out of ten tasks right.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.title: Celebrate small steps
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.text: Don't compare yourself with others. Compare yourself with yourself a month ago. Every new word is a step.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.why: Anyone who sees their progress keeps learning. Small goals that you really reach keep you going longer than one big goal that's far away.
wissen.lernen.sum.title: In short
wissen.lernen.sum.1: Try it yourself first – even if you get it wrong.
wissen.lernen.sum.2: After every mistake, look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.sum.3: Better a little every day than a lot once.
wissen.lernen.sum.4: Mix the topics and speak out loud.
wissen.lernen.studies.title: The studies
wissen.lernen.studies.lead: The asterisks (*) in the text lead here. The studies are in English.
wissen.lernen.study.schultz: The brain signals the difference between expectation and outcome – this error signal steers learning.
wissen.lernen.study.rumelhart: Artificial neural networks learn by correcting their connections a little after every error.
wissen.lernen.study.hebb: Nerve cells that are often active at the same time connect more strongly – the basic idea behind the “beaten path”.
wissen.lernen.study.bengtsson: A lot of practice changes the nerve pathways themselves (the white matter).
wissen.lernen.study.draganski: After three months of juggling, adults' grey matter grew – and shrank back when they stopped.
wissen.lernen.study.boyke: The same works for people around 60, too.
wissen.lernen.study.maguire: London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus – the longer in the job, the clearer it is.
wissen.lernen.study.kornell: Guessing wrong first and then seeing the answer helps more than reading the answer straight away.
wissen.lernen.study.butterfield: Mistakes you were sure about are remembered especially well after they are corrected.
wissen.lernen.study.metcalfe: Overview: mistakes that get corrected help learning instead of harming it.
wissen.lernen.study.roediger: Quizzing yourself keeps knowledge longer than reading it again.
wissen.lernen.study.cepeda: Reviewing with breaks in between beats learning in one go.
wissen.lernen.study.rasch: During sleep the brain consolidates what was learned during the day.
wissen.lernen.study.rohrer: Mixed tasks did clearly better in the later test than tasks in blocks.
wissen.lernen.study.macleod: Words read aloud are remembered better than words read silently.
wissen.lernen.study.bjork: “Desirable difficulties”: what feels hard while practising often stays longer.
wissen.lernen.study.wilson: Learning models make the fastest progress when they get about 85% of the tasks right.

wortfallen.lead: Some words look like a word you already know, or almost like another Portuguese word, and mean something completely different. Here are {n} traps, each with a memory trick.
wortfallen.atualmente.react: So you're not from Lisbon right now? Where will you be from tomorrow?
wortfallen.atualmente.tip: False friend for English speakers (also Spanish actualmente, French actuellement, Italian attualmente). atualmente = now. Actually = na verdade or de facto. The same goes for atual: o preço atual is today's price.
wortfallen.assistir.react: You'll watch your grandmother do the shopping? Or help her carry it?
wortfallen.assistir.tip: False friend for English speakers, and for French (assister). assistir a = to be present at, to watch: assistir a um jogo, a uma aula. To help someone is ajudar. Assistir alguém without a is formal and mostly medical: assistir um doente.
wortfallen.esquisito.react: Odd soup, and you still want the recipe? Brave.
wortfallen.esquisito.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers (exquisito = delicious) and for Italian speakers (squisito). esquisito means strange, weird. For very tasty say delicioso, saboroso or ótimo.
wortfallen.pretender.react: They intend to become pirates? Mind the neighbours.
wortfallen.pretender.tip: False friend for English speakers (to pretend). pretender = to intend, to want to: pretendo mudar de casa. To pretend is fingir. Fingir is the word for acting as if.
wortfallen.fato.react: A habit of pirate? Is that a new kind of hobby?
wortfallen.fato.tip: False friend for English speakers (costume). In Portugal a suit or a costume is o fato (o fato de treino = tracksuit, o fato de banho = swimsuit). o costume is a habit, a custom: Tenho o costume de acordar cedo. Careful: o facto (with c) = the fact. In Brazil fato is the fact and a costume is a fantasia.
wortfallen.puxar.react: Pull towards you? Then the wardrobe won't go to the wall.
wortfallen.puxar.tip: False friend for French speakers: pousser looks like puxar, but pousser = push = empurrar. puxar = to pull. On a door in Portugal, Puxe means pull, Empurre means push.
wortfallen.caldo.react: A broth beach? The sun has been busy.
wortfallen.caldo.tip: False friend for Italian speakers (caldo = hot). In Portuguese o caldo is broth (caldo verde, caldo de galinha). Heat is o calor, and está calor / está quente means it's hot.
wortfallen.burro.react: A toast with a donkey? The café is more adventurous than we thought.
wortfallen.burro.tip: False friend for Italian speakers (burro = butter). In Portuguese o burro is the donkey, and calling someone burro means stupid. Butter is a manteiga.
wortfallen.ginasio.react: She studies at the gym? That's a lot of exercise before exams.
wortfallen.ginasio.tip: False friend for German speakers: das Gymnasium is the escola secundária in Portugal (liceu is the older word). o ginásio is where you train.
wortfallen.taxa.react: A rate of tea? Sounds like a plan for the stock exchange.
wortfallen.taxa.tip: False friend for German speakers (Tasse). a taxa is a fee or a rate: a taxa de juro, a taxa de IVA. A cup is a chávena (in Brazil: a xícara).
wortfallen.renda.react: So your grandmother is a landlady? Good for her!
wortfallen.renda.tip: False friend for German speakers (die Rente = pension). In Portugal a renda is the rent you pay your landlord (o senhorio). The pension is a reforma (also pensão). A reforma can also mean a renovation or reform, so the context decides.
wortfallen.concurso.m1: contest, public tender or public competition
wortfallen.concurso.react: A contest closed the shop? Who won?
wortfallen.concurso.tip: False friend for German speakers (der Konkurs = bankruptcy) and a sneaky one for Italian speakers. In Portuguese o concurso is a contest, a public job competition (concurso público) or a tender. Bankruptcy is a falência.
wortfallen.polvo.react: Cleaning the octopus off the shelf? That's a very tidy sea creature.
wortfallen.polvo.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers: polvo = dust in Spanish, but in Portuguese it's the octopus (polvo à lagareiro is a classic dish). Dust is o pó.
wortfallen.oficina.react: A workshop with computers and meetings? Sounds like a very strange garage.
wortfallen.oficina.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers: oficina = office in Spanish. In Portuguese a oficina is a workshop, and a oficina de automóveis is a garage. An office is um escritório.
wortfallen.rato.react: Wait a mouse? Which one? Is it hiding?
wortfallen.rato.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers: un rato = a while. In Portuguese o rato is the animal (and the computer mouse). A short time is um momento, um bocadinho or um instante.
wortfallen.embaracado.react: Embarrassed for five months? Poor sister.
wortfallen.embaracado.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers (embarazada = pregnant) and a different trap for English speakers. embaraçado means embarrassed or tangled. Pregnant is grávida.
wortfallen.propina.react: A tuition fee for the waiter? He will study well.
wortfallen.propina.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers: propina = tip in Spanish. In Portugal a propina is the tuition fee at a university or school. A tip for a waiter is a gorjeta.
wortfallen.largo.react: Wide hair? It must be a very impressive hairstyle.
wortfallen.largo.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers (largo = long in Spanish). In Portuguese largo means wide, and a largo is also a small square. Long is comprido.
wortfallen.pegar.m1: to take hold of, to catch
wortfallen.pegar.react: Don't pick up the dog? He's tiny. You could even carry him.
wortfallen.pegar.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers (pegar = to hit). In Portuguese pegar means to take hold of, to catch (pegar num livro, pegar fogo) and also to stick. To hit is bater.
wortfallen.cena.react: What is for scene today? A drama, I suppose.
wortfallen.cena.tip: False friend for Spanish and Italian speakers (cena = dinner). In Portuguese a cena is a scene in a film, and colloquially a thing or a situation. The evening meal is o jantar.
wortfallen.atender.react: You've been serving the bus for twenty minutes? It must have been a long queue.
wortfallen.atender.tip: False friend for French speakers (attendre = to wait). atender = to answer (the phone, the door) or to serve a customer: Atende o telefone? Waiting is esperar por or estar à espera de.
wortfallen.sensivel.react: A sensitive man who never loses his head? Interesting.
wortfallen.sensivel.tip: False friend for English speakers (sensible). sensível means sensitive (and perceptible). Sensible is sensato or ajuizado.
wortfallen.realizar.m1: to carry out, to achieve, to hold
wortfallen.realizar.react: You carried out that you lost your passport? Quite an achievement.
wortfallen.realizar.tip: False friend for English speakers (to realize). realizar = to carry out, to make happen: realizar um sonho, realizar uma reunião. To realize (suddenly) is perceber or dar-se conta de.
wortfallen.parentes.react: Your mother and your father are... distant cousins?
wortfallen.parentes.tip: False friend for English and French speakers (parents). Portuguese parentes = relatives (tios, primos, avós). Mother and father together are os pais.
wortfallen.palestra.react: A reading about the history of Lisbon? Bring a book, then.
wortfallen.palestra.tip: False friend for English speakers (lecture). a leitura is the act of reading. A talk or a public lecture is a palestra; a university lecture is an aula.
wortfallen.colegio.react: Engineering in a school? Plenty of homework, then.
wortfallen.colegio.tip: False friend for English speakers (college). In Portugal um colégio is usually a private school for children and teenagers. College is a faculdade or universidade.
wortfallen.constipado.react: A cold? Then why are you talking about the toilet?
wortfallen.constipado.tip: False friend for English and French speakers (constipé). In Portugal estar constipado means you have a cold (a constipação). Constipation is prisão de ventre. At the doctor's, this one matters.
wortfallen.exito.react: You want to find success? Everyone does, but not at this station.
wortfallen.exito.tip: False friend for English speakers (exit). o êxito = success: O filme teve muito êxito. An exit is a saída (also: sair = to leave). Spanish éxito means success too; Italian esito is a result, an outcome.
wortfallen.camara.react: A town hall in the hotel? Hmm, the mayor must be a guest.
wortfallen.camara.tip: False friend for Italian speakers (camera = room). A câmara is the town hall (a Câmara Municipal), the chamber, or a video camera. A room is um quarto; a bedroom is um quarto de dormir.
wortfallen.guardar.m1: to keep, to put away, to save
wortfallen.guardar.react: You'll keep the television for the night? Where will you put it?
wortfallen.guardar.tip: False friend for Italian speakers (guardare = to watch). In Portuguese guardar means to keep or to put away: Guarda o passaporte num sítio seguro. To watch is ver (or olhar para).

hs.about.p: Hamsti’s Bird Safari practises listening and vocabulary at the same time: you hear each noun with its o or a and have to recognise it quickly. Reloading brings o / a and picture questions. All words come from our vocabulary – you can also practise them there at your own pace.
