schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.0: “Nome próprio” is your first name; “apelido” is your surname. Portuguese people often have two or more surnames: put them all in “Apelido(s)”. A form that only asks for “Nome completo” wants everything in one field.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.1: The date is day/month/year: 04/03/1996. 03/04/1996 would be 3 April.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.2: A Portuguese postal code has four digits, a hyphen and three digits (4999-012), and the “localidade” (town) goes in a separate field, even if they are together in the text.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.0: All four points are there: in an exam, a missing point costs more than a small grammar mistake.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.1: There is a greeting and a sign-off (Olá, Catarina! / Um abraço).
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.2: With a friend you use “tu” (“pago-te”). The pronoun goes after the verb, joined with a hyphen: “pago-te”, not “te pago”.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.3: The sentences are short. At A1, “Tenho de trabalhar.” is better than a long sentence with a mistake.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.0: The requests are questions (“Podia…?”, “Importa-se de…?”), not orders (“Regue as minhas plantas”, “Tem de…”).
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.1: After “Importa-se de…?” comes the infinitive: “Importa-se de recolher a minha correspondência?”.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.2: Formal address all the way through: no subject, third person (“Podia…”, “levo-lhe”), and “Dona Amélia” instead of “tu” or just her name. One “podes” in the middle would stand out.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.3: Greeting and sign-off match: “Bom dia, Dona Amélia,” → “Cumprimentos,”. “Beijinhos” is too familiar for a neighbour you hardly know.
schreiben.check.a2-email-school.0: “Está doente” with “estar”, because being ill is a state: “é doente” is a typical mistake.
schreiben.check.a2-email-school.1: The teacher can tell at once which child and which class it is about.
schreiben.check.a2-email-school.2: A polite question: “Podia dizer-me…?”. Parents normally speak to teachers in the formal third person (“a professora”, “podia”); “tu” would be too familiar in a first message.
schreiben.check.a2-email-school.3: In Portugal people say “ir à escola” (with “à”, a + a) and “trabalhos de casa” (or “TPC”); the pronoun after the verb is joined with a hyphen: “dizer-me”.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.0: Numbers are spoken, not written: “vinte de novembro de mil novecentos e oitenta e oito” → 20/11/1988. Phone numbers are often said in groups or digit by digit: “novecentos, zero zero zero, trezentos e quinze” → 900 000 315 (a made-up number).
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.1: “Número de utente” is the number you get when you register with the national health service (SNS). The one in the text is made up; the nine digits are said one by one.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.2: Careful with “Primeira consulta?”. He answers “Não” to a different question (“Já cá veio antes?”), so here the right answer is “sim”.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.3: “Perfeito” means the appointment is confirmed, so fill in the doctor, the date and the time. “Às três e meia da tarde” is 15:30.
schreiben.a2-junta-form.blurb: A practice version of a form you may really meet. Every Junta has its own, so check yours.
schreiben.check.a2-junta-form.0: A Portuguese address runs street, number, floor, side: “Rua das Eiras, n.º 5, 1.º B”. Instead of a letter, the side can be “Esq.” (left) or “Dto.” (right).
schreiben.check.a2-junta-form.1: “Residência anterior” asks where you lived before: Faro, not Valdelora and not Tânger. “Naturalidade” is the place you were born.
schreiben.check.a2-junta-form.2: Copy your NIF exactly, digit by digit. The number here is a placeholder, not a real NIF. “Agregado familiar” means the people who live together in the household.
schreiben.check.a2-junta-form.3: This is language practice, not official guidance: what a Junta de Freguesia asks for (documents, witnesses, a fee) varies, so ask at your own Junta.
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.0: All four points are there, and the landlady can act on them: what is broken, since when, when someone can come.
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.1: The tenses tell the story: “avariou na segunda-feira” (one event) and “não temos” after “desde então” (still true now).
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.2: Formal address throughout (“a senhora”, “podia”, “Escrevo-lhe”), and a comma after the greeting: “Exma. Senhora D. Isabel Antunes,”. In Portuguese emails and letters the greeting normally ends with a comma, not a colon.
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.3: “Prefere que o chame eu”: “preferir que” takes the present subjunctive, and the pronoun goes before the verb after “que” (“que o chame”), but after the verb in a plain sentence (“Escrevo-lhe”).
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.0: A solution comes with the request: the boss reads “posso trocar o turno com o Jorge” and only has to say yes.
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.1: “Tu” with your boss is normal in many Portuguese workplaces, but not all. If yours uses “a senhora”, “a Doutora” or a title, keep to it: “Escrevo-lhe para lhe pedir…”. “Você” is used less in Portugal than in Brazil and can sound distant, so people often use the name or the third person instead.
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.2: The tone is a request, not an announcement: “Se te parecer bem” softens it, and “Podes dizer-me…?” asks instead of ordering. The pronouns follow the verb: “Escrevo-te”, “dizer-me”.
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.3: Time off for official appointments depends on your contract and the law on justified absences; this task practises the email, not your rights. Ask HR or your employer what applies to you.
schreiben.check.b2-beschwerde-reiseveran: No angry words: “Lamento informar que surgiram vários problemas graves” instead of “é uma vergonha”. At B2 the tone is part of the mark: firm, but never rude.
Each problem is set against a promise (“No folheto de V. Exas., … era descrito como… No entanto, na realidade…”). A complaint without that comparison is only an opinion.
There is a clear demand AND a deadline. Without a date, a letter of complaint is not complete.

B2 linking words and forms: “dado que”, “além disso”, “no entanto”, “por isso”, “sem que” + subjunctive. “V. Exas.” (Vossas Excelências) is the formal way to address a company; “Exmos. Senhores,” with a comma, then “Com os melhores cumprimentos”.

In formal European Portuguese, a pronoun with a future verb goes in the middle of it (mesoclisis): “ver-me-ei obrigada”. Many writers avoid it (“terei de apresentar…”), but you should be able to read and use it. Whether a business must offer the “Livro de Reclamações” (also online) is a rule to check before you rely on it.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.0: The position is clear in the first paragraph, and the last paragraph comes back to it.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.1: Each argument has an example of its own. “Seria mais seguro” alone is a claim; the two streets on the way to school make it real.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.2: The other side gets a fair sentence before the answer: “É verdade que…; no entanto…”.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.3: B2 forms: the conditional for what would happen (“melhoraria”, “ganharia”), “não se trata de…, mas de…”, “prefiro que” + present subjunctive (“sirvam”). Note “autocarro” and “estacionamento”: these are the words used in Portugal.
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.0: Every field is filled in. An empty field counts as a mistake, even if the information is in the text.
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.1: Copy names, numbers and dates exactly as they are in the text, with their accents; in Portugal the day comes before the month (12 de setembro, 12/09).
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.2: Nothing made up: if something is not in the text, leave the field empty or put a dash.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.0: Every point in the task is covered. A missing point costs more than three grammar mistakes.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.1: Greeting and sign-off suit each other and the person (Olá, Tiago! … Um abraço; Exmo. Senhor … Com os melhores cumprimentos).
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.2: The sentences are linked (por isso, porque, mas, além disso, embora), not just one after the other.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.0: Read first, then compare: discuss the text only once you have marked every mistake you can find.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.1: The text has about 20 mistakes. Look at: ser or estar, gender, “desde” or “há”, irregular verb forms, where the pronoun goes after “não”, agreement with “ninguém”, “bom” or “bem”, the subjunctive after “gostava que”, a capital letter on a month, “você” in a formal letter, and two closing lines translated word for word from English.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.2: Write down the mistakes you make yourself, too. That is the point of the task.
ac.find.rr: “{word}” has r: a single r between vowels is one quick tap; rr and a first r are the strong r at the back of the mouth. caro is not carro.
ac.find.jg: “{word}”: j, and g before e or i, is like the s in “measure”. Not a rasp, and not the j of “jam”.
ac.find.nasal: “{word}”: the vowel is nasal. Let the air go through your nose, and don't finish with a clear n or m.
ac.find.ch: “{word}” has ch: it is sh, as in “shop”. Not ch as in “church”, and not k.
ac.find.enlace: “{word}” follows straight on from the word before. No small stop in your throat.
ac.find.doble: “{word}”: the consonants are short. Don't hold them; move straight on to the next vowel.
ac.find.reducao: “{word}”: an unstressed e is very weak (a short “ɨ” or nothing at all). Don't say a full e. pequeno is nearly “p'keno”.
ac.find.ou: “{word}” ends in o: an unstressed final o sounds like u. livro is “livru”.
ac.find.abertas: “{word}”: listen to the accent. é and ó are open, ê and ô are closed. avó and avô are different people.
ac.find.ao: “{word}” has a nasal diphthong. Start with the nasal vowel and glide on to a short w or y, with no real n.
ac.find.ssh: “{word}”: s before a consonant or at the end of a word sounds like sh (like the s in “measure” before b, d, g, m, n, l, r, v). luz is “loosh”.
ac.find.sz: “{word}”: s between vowels buzzes like z; ss and ç are a sharp s. casa is not caça.
ac.find.lhnh: “{word}” has lh or nh: one sound each, made with the middle of the tongue against the roof of the mouth, like “million” or “canyon”.
ac.find.lfinal: “{word}”: l at the end of a syllable is dark, said with the back of the tongue raised, almost like a short “w”.
satzmelodie.rule.cortes: In Portugal a polite request is often a question with pode or podia, or a statement with queria. The voice rises gently at the end, and se faz favor or por favor does the rest.

nat.entry.blurb: Residence permit, CIPLE A2 and nationality: who needs what, who is exempt, and the steps in order.
nat.link.more: How nationality by residence works, step by step
nat.title: Residence and nationality in Portugal: the path
nat.lead: To get permanent residence or Portuguese nationality, most adults need years of legal residence and proof of Portuguese at level A2, usually the CIPLE certificate. Here is who needs what, who is exempt, what changed recently and in what order to do things.
nat.legal: General orientation, not legal advice. Portugal's immigration and nationality rules changed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 and may have changed again since. We wrote this page from general knowledge of the rules and have not checked every point against the official texts, so every number and rule here is marked to verify in our notes. Check the official pages listed at the end, or ask a lawyer, before you decide anything.
nat.short.title: The short version
nat.short.1: You live in Portugal legally, with a residence permit or an EU registration, and you keep proof of it.
nat.short.2: After enough years of legal residence (the time depends on the route and the law in force) you can ask for permanent residence or for nationality.
nat.short.3: For both, most adults must show Portuguese at A2: usually a CIPLE certificate, unless they are exempt or another proof is accepted.
nat.short.4: For nationality you also need clean criminal records, official documents from your country and a fee. The decision can take a long time.
nat.perm.title: Before nationality: the residence permit
nat.perm.1: Non-EU residents get a residence permit (autorização de residência) from AIMA, the agency that took over most of the old SEF's immigration work in October 2023. A first permit is temporary and has to be renewed.
nat.perm.2: EU citizens register at their town hall (câmara municipal) after three months and get a registration certificate instead of a permit.
nat.perm.3: A permanent residence permit usually needs about five years of legal residence, A2 Portuguese, housing and enough income. Check the exact conditions with AIMA.
nat.perm.4: You also need the basics of everyday life in order: a tax number (NIF), a social security number (NISS), a health user number (número de utente) and a certificate of residence from your Junta de Freguesia. They are not the same as legal residence, but offices ask for them.
nat.res.title: How long you must have lived in Portugal
nat.res.gen.time: About 5 years: the general rule so far
nat.res.gen.who: Adults who have lived in Portugal legally for the time the law asks for, counted by rules that AIMA and the registry office apply (when the clock starts is a known point of dispute: to verify). In 2025 parliament debated and voted longer periods, around 7 years for nationals of Portuguese-speaking countries and 10 years for others. Parts of that reform were challenged in court. Check which period applies on the day you apply.
nat.res.spouse.time: About 3 years: marriage or de facto partnership
nat.res.spouse.who: People married to a Portuguese national, or in a registered de facto partnership (união de facto), usually apply by declaration after about three years, and have to show real ties to Portugal. Details and recent changes: to verify.
nat.res.desc.who: Grandchildren of a Portuguese national, and some other descendants born abroad, can apply by declaration if they show real ties to the Portuguese community. Proof of Portuguese is part of this: to verify.
nat.res.born.who: Children born in Portugal to foreign parents can get nationality depending on the parents' legal residence. The required time was shortened in 2022 and may be different now: to verify.
nat.res.seph.who: The route for descendants of Sephardic Jews expelled from Portugal was tightened in 2022 and, as far as we know, closed to new applications in 2024. Check the registry office if you are in this situation.
nat.res.note: Residence has to be legal. Time without a valid permit or registration generally does not count, and long absences can cause problems. Keep your permits, renewals, tax returns and social security records together, because you will need to prove the years.
nat.tests.title: Who needs proof of Portuguese
nat.t.most.who: Most adults applying for nationality or permanent residence
nat.t.ciple.who: You already hold a CIPLE or a higher CAPLE certificate
nat.t.ciple.proof: That is the proof: no new exam
nat.t.cplp.who: You are a national of a country where Portuguese is an official language (Brazil, Angola, Cape Verde, Mozambique and others)
nat.t.cplp.proof: Often accepted without a CIPLE, with documents from your country: ask which ones
nat.t.school.who: You went to school in Portugal, or have another school certificate in Portuguese that is accepted
nat.t.school.proof: Can replace the exam: ask how to submit it
nat.t.test.who: You take the Portuguese test for nationality or permanent residence offered by authorised centres
nat.t.test.proof: Accepted as an alternative to the CIPLE as far as we know: to verify
nat.t.minor.proof: Usually exempt or a different rule applies
nat.t.disp.who: You cannot read or write, or you have a disability or illness that makes a test impossible
nat.t.disp.proof: Ask the authority about an exemption before you apply
nat.list.title: What CIPLE is, and what to check
nat.list.text: CIPLE is the A2 level of the CAPLE exams (ACESSO A1, CIPLE A2, DEPLE B1, DIPLE B2, DAPLE C1, DUPLE C2). It tests reading, writing, listening and speaking at an everyday level. Exam centres run it on fixed dates in Portugal and abroad.
nat.list.warn: Before you book, ask the office that handles your application which proofs it accepts, whether A2 is enough for your route, and whether a certificate can be too old. We could not confirm these points (to verify).
nat.steps.title: The steps, in order
nat.s1.title: 1. Get and keep legal residence
nat.s1.text: Apply for your permit or EU registration, renew on time and keep every document. The years of legal residence are what everything else is built on.
nat.s2.title: 2. Find out which route and which language proof apply to you
nat.s2.text: Residence by the general rule, marriage, descent or birth in Portugal each have different conditions. Find out whether you need a CIPLE or are exempt, and ask for an exemption in good time if you think you qualify.
nat.s3.title: 3. Take CIPLE A2 (or another accepted proof)
nat.s3.text: Register with an authorised exam centre, and book early because dates are limited and results take a while. Preparing with a course, our mock and some speaking practice is usually enough for A2. No course is compulsory as far as we know.
nat.s4.title: 4. Collect your documents
nat.s4.text: Expect to need your passport, your residence permit, your birth certificate and a criminal record certificate from your country of origin (often with an apostille and a sworn translation), a Portuguese criminal record certificate, your NIF and proof of your language level. The exact list changes, so use the checklist on the official application page.
nat.s5.title: 5. Apply and pay the fee
nat.s5.text: Nationality applications are handled by the registry service (IRN, the Instituto dos Registos e do Notariado), online or at a registry office (Conservatória). The fee for naturalisation was around €250 at the time of writing: to verify.
nat.s6.title: 6. Wait for the decision
nat.s6.text: Processing has taken a year or more in many cases, and the legal deadlines have not always been met. Keep your contact details up to date and answer any request for documents quickly. If your residence permit expires while you wait, ask what to do.
nat.s7.title: 7. Register, then get your Cartão de Cidadão and passport
nat.s7.text: If your application is approved, the nationality is registered. As far as we know there is no oath ceremony, but check. After that you can apply for the Cartão de Cidadão (citizen card) and a Portuguese passport. A residence card is for residents, the Cartão de Cidadão is for citizens.
nat.s7.after: Portugal allows dual nationality, but whether your first country still treats you as a citizen depends on its own law, so ask its consulate.
nat.other: This page only covers the main routes. Nationality for other situations has its own rules, and so does the residence of people from specific countries (for example the CPLP mobility agreement).
nat.changes.title: What changed recently
nat.changes.1: October 2023: SEF was dissolved. AIMA took over residence permits, and the police took over border and police work.
nat.changes.2: June 2024: the manifestação de interesse route, a way to start a residence process from inside Portugal, ended.
nat.changes.3: 2022 and 2024: the Sephardic route was tightened and then, as far as we know, closed.
nat.changes.4: 2025: a reform of the nationality law was debated and voted, with longer residence periods and, possibly, extra requirements such as a culture or civics knowledge test. Parts were challenged in court. What is in force when you apply is what counts.

dgt.orient.title: The driving licence in Portugal: a short orientation
dgt.orient.legal: General orientation, not legal advice. Rules and exam details change. This is how we understood them in November 2026; check the official IMT website (Instituto da Mobilidade e dos Transportes, the road transport authority) before you rely on them.
dgt.orient.1: To get a new licence (carta de condução), you pass a theory exam (exame teórico, or o código) and a practical exam (exame de condução). Most people go to a driving school (escola de condução), which also arranges the learner's licence and the exam dates.
dgt.orient.2: You also need a medical certificate (atestado médico) before you apply.
dgt.orient.3: The licence works with points (carta por pontos), and fines (coimas) for traffic offences are handled by the ANSR. Check the current rules on the IMT and ANSR websites.
dgt.orient.4: You may not have to take the theory exam in Portuguese. Ask your driving school or the IMT which languages are offered for the exam, and check this before you register. Even then, signs, instructions and papers will be in Portuguese.
dgt.orient.5: If you already hold a licence from another country, you may be able to use or exchange it (troca de carta) instead of taking the exams. Licences from EU/EEA countries are usually valid, while other licences may have to be exchanged within a period after you become resident. It depends on the country and your situation, so check yours with the IMT first.
dgt.orient.practice: For practice questions, use the IMT's own material or your driving school's tests.

kultur.duzen-siezen.cardIntro: In Portugal you use tu with friends, family, children and people of your own age, and o senhor or a senhora with older strangers and in offices.
kultur.pfand.cardIntro: In Portugal people greet with a word first, and often with a touch: dois beijinhos (two light kisses on the cheeks) or a handshake.
kultur.sonntagsruhe.cardIntro: In Portugal lunch is usually between about 12:30 and 2 pm, and dinner often starts around 8 pm.
kultur.trinkgeld.cardIntro: In a Portuguese café you often order at the counter, and a small coffee is very cheap.
kultur.bundeslaender.cardIntro: Portugal is made up of the mainland (o continente) and two groups of islands in the Atlantic, the Azores (os Açores) and Madeira, which are autonomous regions.
kultur.feiertage.cardIntro: Portugal has 13 national public holidays (feriados nacionais), and every município adds one municipal holiday of its own.
kultur.comida.cardIntro: Meals in Portugal have their own names: o pequeno-almoço, o almoço, o lanche and o jantar.
kultur.fiestas.cardIntro: In June, many Portuguese towns celebrate the Santos Populares (the popular saints) with music, grilled sardines and street parties.
kultur.fado.cardIntro: Fado is a song style from Portugal, sung by one voice with the guitarra portuguesa and a classical guitar.
kultur.muelltrennung.cardIntro: In Portugal you sort your rubbish into the ecoponto, a group of coloured containers in the street.
kultur.termine.cardIntro: At many public offices in Portugal you are served by number: you take a senha (a ticket) and wait until it is called.
kultur.anmeldung.cardIntro: When you start a life in Portugal, you collect a few numbers and papers that almost every office, employer and landlord will ask for.
kultur.krankenversicherung.cardIntro: Portugal has a national health service, the Serviço Nacional de Saúde (SNS), which is paid for mainly through taxes.
kultur.mieten.cardIntro: In Portugal a rental is based on a written contrato de arrendamento between you and the senhorio or senhoria (landlord).
kultur.schulsystem.cardIntro: In Portugal school is compulsory from the age of 6 until 18, or until the student finishes the 12.º ano (year 12).
kultur.arbeit-finden.cardIntro: In Portugal people find work through job websites, personal contacts and the public employment service, the IEFP (Instituto do Emprego e Formação Profissional).
kultur.lenguas-cooficiales.cardIntro: Portuguese is the official language of Portugal and the first language of almost everyone who grows up there.
kultur.mundo-hispano.cardIntro: Portuguese is an official language in nine countries on four continents, and most of its speakers live in Brazil.
kultur.ausbildung.cardIntro: After secondary school, Portugal offers two kinds of higher education, universidades and institutos politécnicos, as well as vocational training.
kultur.kuendigung.cardIntro: How a job ends in Portugal decides what you are owed and whether you can get unemployment benefit.
RTP (Rádio e Televisão de Portugal) is Portugal's public broadcaster, with television channels, radio stations and a free online platform.
kultur.vereine.cardIntro: In Portugal a lot of local life happens in associações: cultural and sports clubs, music bands, folk dance groups and, very often, the volunteer fire brigade.
kultur.tradiciones-america.cardIntro: The Portuguese-speaking countries share a language, but each has its own music, festivals and food.
kultur.foederalismus.cardIntro: Portugal is a unitary state, not a federation: laws for the whole country are made in Lisbon, and only the Azores and Madeira have their own regional parliaments and governments.
kultur.sozialversicherung.cardIntro: The Segurança Social is the public system that pays pensions, sick pay, parental pay, unemployment benefit and family allowances.
kultur.wahlen.cardIntro: In Portugal you vote for party lists in parliamentary elections and directly for a person in presidential elections.
kultur.historia-compartida.cardIntro: Portugal and the other Portuguese-speaking countries share more than five centuries of history, from the sea voyages of the 15th century to the independence of the African colonies in the 1970s.
kultur.erinnerungskultur.cardIntro: On 25 April 1974 a military coup ended almost fifty years of dictatorship in Portugal, and the day became known as the Revolução dos Cravos (Carnation Revolution).
kultur.grundgesetz.cardIntro: The Constituição da República Portuguesa was approved on 2 April 1976 and came into force on 25 April 1976, two years after the revolution.
kultur.mitbestimmung.cardIntro: In Portugal workers' rights come from the Constitution, the Código do Trabalho and the collective agreement (convenção coletiva) of your sector.

ap.hint.title.text: Learning gender through rules only takes you so far, because many rules have exceptions. What works best is learning every noun together with its article (a mesa, o livro, a mão), for example in the vocabulary trainer, and then meeting the words in everyday life. Treat the rules as help with a new word. The most reliable ones: -dade, -tude, -ção, -são and -agem → a (a cidade, a atitude, a estação, a viagem; a well-known exception: o coração); most words in -ema and -ama from Greek → o (o problema, o sistema, o programa).
ap.regel.intro: Every Portuguese noun is masculine or feminine, and the article shows which: o or a. The ending of the noun is often a reliable clue. These patterns help when you meet a new word, but they have exceptions, so learn each noun with its article.
ap.regel.people: With people and some animals the article follows the person: o médico / a médica, o estudante / a estudante. For many words there is no pattern at all, and the article simply has to be learned with the word.
ap.ex.greek: “{word}” is one of the words in -ma that come from Greek. They take “o”, unlike a cama or a forma: o {word}.

delesiele.p.nationality.title: Residence and nationality in Portugal
delesiele.p.nationality.text: For the language proof in a residence or nationality application, the usual exam is the CIPLE, level A2 of the CAPLE certificates, taken at an exam centre approved by CAPLE (University of Lisbon). Some people are exempt, and other proofs, such as a school certificate, can count in some procedures. The rules and the accepted levels changed in 2024–2025, so ask the office that handles your case (AIMA, the Conservatória dos Registos Centrais) before you book. To verify.
delesiele.p.work.title: Work
delesiele.p.work.text: Employers in Portugal usually care about your level more than the name of the exam. A CIPLE or DEPLE certificate is a clear, recognised proof. Regulated professions and public jobs can set a level, such as B1 or B2, so read the call for applications. A Brazilian employer or a company working with Brazil may know the Celpe-Bras better. To verify for your case.
delesiele.p.university.title: University and study
delesiele.p.university.text: Portuguese universities that need proof of Portuguese often ask for B1 or B2, which points to the DEPLE or DIPLE. Some run their own Portuguese courses and tests instead. Brazilian universities and programmes for foreign students often ask for the Celpe-Bras. Each institution sets its own rule, so get it in writing. To verify.
delesiele.p.brazil.title: Brazil or Portugal?
delesiele.p.brazil.answer: Pick the country you will live in
delesiele.p.brazil.text: The two exams are built for two varieties. The CAPLE exams are written for European Portuguese and are the ones the Portuguese authorities know. The Celpe-Bras is Brazil's exam and is set around Brazilian usage. A certificate from one country is not automatically accepted in the other. Check with the office that will read your result. To verify.
delesiele.p.self.title: For yourself
delesiele.p.self.text: If you want a goal at a level you choose, the CAPLE exams give you one certificate per level, from A1 to C2. The Celpe-Bras does not work like that: you take one exam, and the result is a level of the Brazilian scale, if you reach one.
